title: The first screen of a CRM
metaTitle: The first screen of a CRM
excerpt: Between calls, a salesperson needs the next record and one action. The first screen should name that object, not open with a product tour.
alt: Clothes on wooden hangers suspended from a white branch against a plain wall, a few pieces set out so the next choice is obvious.
caption: A few garments on hangers, ready to be chosen without a tour of the closet. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first screen of a CRM show?
faqs.answer: Show the next useful object for the salesperson who is updating a record between calls, and name one action. That object is usually the account, the deal, or the call they just finished. A tour, a chart of the whole pipeline, and a row of tips can wait until someone asks for them.

faqs.question: Is a dashboard a good first screen?
faqs.answer: A dashboard answers how the quarter is going, which is a manager's question, not the job between calls. The person with two minutes needs a record and a place to write what just happened. Give managers their view without making everyone land there.

faqs.question: How do we know the first screen is right?
faqs.answer: Watch someone use it in the gap between two real calls, or a timed rehearsal of that gap. If they can name the object and complete the one action without opening a menu, the screen is working. If they ask where to put the note, it is not.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
CRM UX on the first screen is a single decision: show the next useful object, not a tour. Name the object and the one action. The person in front of it is a salesperson updating a record between calls. They do not have a minute to be onboarded again.

If the screen cannot be understood in the time it takes the next call to start ringing, it is the wrong screen.

## The gap between two calls

The gap is short, slightly stressful, and full of a fact that will evaporate. What the buyer said. Whether the deal moved. When to call back. The product's job is to catch that fact and attach it to the right record before the next conversation begins. Everything else is a hobby the product is imposing on someone who did not consent.

Design for that gap before you design for the quarterly review. The review has a chair and a coffee. The gap has a laptop on a knee, or a phone, and a name half-remembered. The first screen should assume the review is not happening. It should assume the note is.

[Nielsen Norman Group's research on how long people stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is about web pages, and the lesson transfers. People often leave in 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is obvious immediately. A salesperson will not "leave" their CRM in the middle of a workday. They will abandon the note. They will type it into a personal scratch pad, or they will trust their memory, and the record will be wrong by evening. The first screen has to communicate its value in those first seconds: here is the record, here is where the note goes.

Do not open with a modal that welcomes them back. Do not open with a changelog. Do not open with a coach mark pointing at a feature you shipped. Those are tours. Tours are what you do to someone who has time. This person does not.

## Name the object

The object is the thing they came to change. Say its name in the heading, in their words. "Northwind, follow-up Thursday" is a name. "Record 44821" is a database being rude. If you know which account they were just on, put that account here. If you do not, the first screen is a short list of the records they are likely to need: the call that just ended, the next meeting, the deal they touched this morning. Not the entire book of business. Not a chart.

One object should be visually first. A heading, the person's or company's name, the next step, and the last note. Supporting facts can sit nearby if they help the note: the role of the person they spoke to, the amount, the stage. Supporting facts that exist because the data model has them, such as a billing address and a lead source from two years ago, belong one tap away. Between calls, extra fields are clutter that looks like work.

Hanabi's public product work, Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai, is useful as a standard of focus rather than as a CRM. The lesson to steal is narrow: one hierarchy, words that say what happens next, a screen a person can scan. A CRM first screen can live up to that. A CRM first screen that is a mosaic of widgets is refusing to choose an object, and the salesperson pays for the indecision every hour.

Empty is a real state. A new hire with no calls yet should not see a fake chart. They should see how a record will look, and the one action that creates their first note. A returning rep with a clear next call should not see the new-hire explanation. Remember who they are. The first screen is allowed to be different for those two people. It is not allowed to be a tour for both.

## One action, labeled as a verb

Pick the verb. "Log this call." "Set the next step." "Save the note." Put that verb on the button they will hit, in the spot their eye reaches after the name. If there are two verbs of equal weight, you have not decided what the gap is for. Choose. The other verb can be present and quiet.

The note field should be ready. A cursor already in the field is a kindness. A field that requires a click, then a mode, then a type of activity selected from a taxonomy of fourteen options, is how notes die. Ask for the type after the words are safe, or infer it. Do not hold the prose hostage to a dropdown.

Label the action with the object. "Save note to Northwind" is harder to mis-tap than "Submit." Submit is a developer's word. The salesperson is not submitting. They are trying not to lose a sentence a buyer said about budget.

Secondary actions, like changing the stage or assigning a teammate, can live on the same record if they are truly part of the same gap. They should not look like the primary button. A screen with four primary buttons has no primary. It has a committee.

## What a tour costs

A tour costs the note. That is the whole accounting. The product tour feels like teaching, and teaching feels virtuous in a design review. In the gap between calls it is an interruption by the tool they opened in order to do the job. People skip tours. Then they skip the field the tour was pointing at. Then the data is thin and a later meeting blames the team for not using the CRM. They were using it. It was talking over them.

If you need to teach, teach on a quiet screen, or in a short empty state the first time they create a record, not on every return. One sentence beside the field beats a five-step overlay. "Write what they said. You can set the stage after." That is teaching. A spotlight on the global navigation is not.

Charts of team performance on this screen are a different product, the manager's. Give the manager a place to open them. Do not staple them to the top of the rep's gap. A rep who sees the team's numbers before the note field will either freeze or ignore both. Neither helps the record.

Also refuse the upsell strip. "Connect your inbox," "invite your team," "try forecasting." Those are the company's goals. The first screen belongs to the user's goal. You can offer those on a settings visit or a true empty day. You cannot offer them in the ninety seconds after a call and still claim the product respects the work.

## Coming back to a record they know

Most opens are not first opens. The salesperson has seen this account before. The first screen should respect memory. Show what changed since they were last here, in one line, then the note field. "Stage moved to proposal by Sam, yesterday." That line prevents a duplicate note and a contradictory one. It is more useful than a hero illustration of a pipeline.

Do not reset their context with a marketing layout. No full-bleed image. No inspirational sentence about selling. The brand of a CRM, at this minute, is whether the note survives. Type, spacing, and a calm button are the brand. Got Next and Leadly are reminders that a product can feel finished without decorating the moment of work. Trade Moai is a reminder that scan order matters. Put the name where a scan starts. Put the action where the scan ends. Do not put a illustration in between.

If they were midway through a note when a call started, restore the draft. Losing a half-written note is a betrayal the product will not be forgiven for, even if the rest of the interface is handsome. Autosave is part of the first screen, not a settings preference buried under "advanced."

## What stays off this screen

Keep off the first screen:

1. A product tour or a changelog.
2. Team dashboards and forecast widgets.
3. Fields that do not help this note.
4. Settings, integrations, and invitations.
5. A search box as the only way in, unless you truly do not know the record.

Search still matters, when the record you assumed is wrong. It should be easy to reach and not be the whole screen. The next essay in this series is about what happens when the save fails. Before that, the screen has to make the save worth attempting.

Navigation belongs at the edge. The record belongs in the middle. If your first screen is mostly navigation, you have designed a lobby. Lobbies are where people get lost on the way to the room they already named.

Test with a timer. Hand a rep a one-sentence outcome from a fake call and start a clock. The note should be on the right record before a minute passes, without help from you. If you have to point, the object was not named, or the action was not the verb. Fix that before you add a single widget. Widgets are how teams avoid this test. The test is cheaper than a quarter of bad data.

## A screen you can defend in a review

In critique, ask one question: what is the object, and what is the verb? If the room cannot answer in a single breath, the screen is still a tour. Strip it back to the name, the last note, the field, and the button. Add a fact only when a rep, in the timed test, asked for it.

That is a smaller screen than the roadmap wanted. It is the screen that gets used. A CRM that is used between calls becomes a record of the truth. A CRM that is admired in a demo and avoided in the gap becomes a place people reconstruct history on Friday, badly.

The build should match that restraint. A Next.js front end, TypeScript, and a clear data model in PostgreSQL will not choose the object for you. They will faithfully render a cluttered first screen if that is what was designed. Choose in Figma, with the gap written at the top of the frame: "between calls." Then remove everything that does not serve the note.

When the note is saved and something goes wrong, the screen has a second job. [Errors in a CRM](/blog/errors-in-a-crm) is the next piece, because a failure between calls has to say what broke and what to do, while the next phone call is already close.

If this is the product you are shaping, [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) shows the kind of interface Hanabi designs and builds, focused enough that the next action is visible.
